blocks.text: A visual representation of the electric field can be obtained in terms of electric field lines, an idea proposed by Michael Faraday. Electric field lines can be considered as a visual map used to represent the direction and strength of an electric field around a charged object. As electric field lines provide information about the electric force exerted on a charged object, these lines are commonly called “electric lines of force”.

To introduce electric field lines, we place positive test charges +q₀ each of magnitude q₀ at different places but at equal distances from a positive charge +q as shown in the Fig. 9.5. Each test charge will experience a repulsive force, as indicated by arrows in Fig. 9.5(a). Therefore, the electric field created by the charge +q is directed radially outward. Figure 9.5(b) shows corresponding field lines which show the field direction. Figure 9.6 shows the electric field lines in the vicinity of a negative charge −q. In this case the lines are directed radially “inward”, because the force on a positive test charge is now of attraction, indicating the electric field points inward.

blocks.alt: (a) Eight small orange test charges +q0 on a dotted circle round a central charge +q; a magenta arrow points radially outward from each. (b) Straight field lines radiating from +q in all directions with arrowheads pointing outward.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.5: (a) A positive test charge +q0 placed anywhere near a positive point charge +q experiences a repulsive force directed radially outward; (b) the field lines are directed radially outward from +q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.5).

blocks.alt: A blue charge -q with straight field lines coming in from all directions; the arrowheads point inward, towards -q.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.6: The electric field lines are directed radially inward towards a negative point charge -q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.6).

blocks.text: Figures 9.5 and 9.6 represent two dimensional pictures of the field lines. However, electric field lines emerge from the charges in three dimensions, and an infinite number of lines could be drawn.

The electric field lines “map” also provides information about the strength of the electric field. As we notice in Figs. 9.5 and 9.6 that field lines are closer to each other near the charges where the field is strong while they continuously spread out indicating a continuous decrease in the field strength.
The number of lines per unit area passing perpendicularly through it is proportional to the magnitude of the electric field.
bold: The number of lines per unit area passing perpendicularly through it is proportional to the magnitude of the electric field.

blocks.text: The electric field lines are curved in case of two identical separated charges. Figure 9.7 shows the pattern of lines associated with two identical positive point charges of equal magnitude. It reveals that the lines in the region between two like charges seem to repel each other. The behaviour of two identical negatively charges will be exactly the same. The middle region shows the presence of a zero field spot or neutral zone.

blocks.alt: Two equal positive charges +q side by side. Field lines leave each charge in all directions and curve away from the other charge; between them the lines bend apart, leaving an empty zero-field spot midway.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.7: The electric field lines for two identical positive point charges (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption of Figure 9.7 calls the charges opposite, but the figure shows two identical positive charges, as captioned above.

Figure 9.8 shows the electric field pattern of two opposite charges of equal magnitudes. The field lines start from positive charge and end on a negative charge. The electric field at points such as 1, 2, 3 is the resultant of fields created by the two charges at these points. The directions of the resultant intensities is given by the tangents drawn to the field lines at these points.

blocks.alt: A positive charge +q (left) and a negative charge -q (right). Field lines leave +q, curve round and end on -q; outer lines leave the picture from +q and others come in from outside to -q. Points 1, 2 and 3 on three lines carry short red arrows along the tangent.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.8: The electric field lines of two opposite charges of equal magnitude (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the caption of Figure 9.6 again under Figure 9.8. This figure shows the field lines of two opposite charges of equal magnitude, as captioned above.

In the regions where the field lines are parallel and equally spaced, the same number of lines pass per unit area and therefore, field is uniform on all points. Figure 9.9 shows the field lines between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The field is uniform in the middle region where field lines are equally spaced.

blocks.alt: Two vertical plates, + on the left and - on the right. Between them parallel, evenly spaced field lines point from + to -. Near the top and bottom edges the lines bulge outward in curves; outside, lines leave the + plate to the left and come in to the - plate from the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.9: In the central region of a parallel plate capacitor, the electric field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, indicating that the electric field there has the same magnitude and direction at points (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.9).

blocks.text: We are now in a position to summarize the properties of electric field lines.

items: Electric field lines originate from positive charges and end on negative charges.
The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field at that point.
The lines are closer where the field is strong and the lines are farther apart where the field is weak.
No two lines cross each other. This is because E has only one direction at any given point. If the lines cross E could have more than one direction.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: There is no electric field inside the conductor.
